Mechanistic Interpretability · Research Report

Reading & controlling sycophancy
in language models

Can we locate where a model decides to flatter the user, read that decision from its activations, and then switch it off — without breaking the model? A guided tour of the full research, ending with the latest result: sycophancy is a multi-dimensional subspace.

GPT-2 · Pythia · Qwen-Instruct Anthropic sycophancy evals probes · steering · subspace ablation

Tab 1The question & the through-line

Sycophancy — telling the user what they want to hear rather than what is true — is a safety-relevant behavior. We asked two things: (a) can we read a model's sycophancy preference from its internal activations, and (b) once we can, can we causally switch it off without degrading the model? The second half is the crux — reading a behavior is not the same as controlling it.

Index

  1. Probe-guided attribution — the intuition, what we measure, the data, and the first three findings Tab 2
  2. Steering & the sycophancy subspace — intervention types with formulas, side-effects, and the multi-dimensional result Tab 3

The research flow — what led to what

  1. Measure the model's own preference. Define behavior_margin and train a probe on the prompt-final activation to predict it. → is the signal real?
  2. It's decodable and replicates. The probe strengthens with depth in both GPT-2 and Pythia. → could it be a trivial confound?
  3. Controls say it's real (clears the random-label floor), and instruct models are more sycophantic (66% vs ~50%). → where do we intervene?
  4. Decoding ≠ causation. The most readable layer is not the most causal one. → intervene at causal layers — but does it have side effects?
  5. Probe-direction steering works but makes the model weird. Capping is clean but does nothing. → maybe sycophancy isn't a single direction.
  6. Sycophancy is a subspace. Removing a rank-2 subspace flips 40% of answers at ~0.03 side-effect — clean and moderately strong. → what are the extra directions?
  7. One direction per topic. The subspace is a union of topic-specific sycophancy directions (political, NLP, philosophy).

Tab 2Probe-guided attribution — intuition, method & data

The intuition

Standard attribution reads a single output-token logit (e.g. the logit for “Yes”). But “Yes” fires in countless harmless contexts — it is a poor proxy for a behavior. Probe-guided attribution instead trains a small linear probe on the model's internal activations to detect the behavior itself, then attributes and intervenes through that probe. It reads the model's state, not one token.

What we measure

For each prompt (a persona stating a view, then a two-choice question) the target is the model's own preference, in log-probabilities:

behavior_margin = mean-token logP(sycophantic answer | prompt) − mean-token logP(honest answer | prompt)

Positive → the model leans sycophantic. We probe the activation at the final prompt token — the instant before it answers — like reading someone's face the moment they finish hearing a loaded question.

The data

Sycophancy (main): Anthropic model-written-evals, three sub-types pooled evenly — philosophy (philpapers2020), NLP researchers (nlp_survey), and politics (political_typology_quiz). Side-effects (capability): 30 authored general-knowledge prompts (“Why is the sky blue?”, “What is 2+2?”), unrelated to sycophancy, used to check interventions don't degrade the model.

Finding 1 — decodable, and it replicates

The probe predicts the behavior margin and gets stronger with depth — the same rising curve in two unrelated model families. Two architectures agreeing points to a real, shared mechanism.

How to read it
x-axis = relative layer depth (0 = first layer, 1 = last), so the two models line up despite different layer counts. y-axis = the probe's held-out test correlation (Pearson r) between predicted and true behavior_margin. Higher = the preference is more linearly readable at that depth.

Finding 2 — it's real, and instruct models are worse

Re-running the identical probe on control targets: a random-label probe (shuffled target = the noise floor) and surface-feature probes. The sycophancy probe (≈0.52) clears the random-label floor (≈0.25) — real signal — but surface features are also decodable, so a confound contribution can't be fully excluded.

Sycophancy is also amplified by post-training: Qwen-Instruct prefers the sycophantic answer 66% of the time vs. ~50% for base models.

Finding 3 — decoding ≠ causation (the pivot)

Sweeping every layer independently, the layer where sycophancy is most readable is not the layer where intervening most changes behavior. Reading and steering live in different places.

How to read it
x-axis = layer index. Left y-axis (blue) = decodability (probe test Pearson). Right y-axis (orange) = causal effect, i.e. |Δ behavior_margin| when that layer's residual is patched. The two curves peaking apart is the whole point: attribute where it's causal, not where it reads.
This set up the next question. Once we intervene at the causal layers to actually change behavior, does the intervention have unintended side effects? That is the subject of Tab 3.

Tab 3Steering & the sycophancy subspace — the latest findings

We now use the probe direction to causally intervene, and — crucially — check whether the intervention harms the model. Below, h is the residual activation at a layer, d̂ a unit sycophancy direction, α a steering strength, and ‖·‖ a vector length.

The five intervention methods (with formulas)

Additive steering — the blunt baseline

h ← h + α · s · d̂   (s = mean residual norm at the layer, so α is in “residual-norms”)

Shove the activation along the sycophancy axis. Problem: it also inflates ‖h‖, drowning out the rest of the computation → the model goes weird.

Norm-preserving additive

h ← (h + α·s·d̂) · ( ‖h‖ / ‖h + α·s·d̂‖ )

Same push, then rescale to the original length — removes the inflation damage.

Activation capping

h ← h − max(0, (h·d̂) − θ) · d̂   (θ = a high quantile of h·d̂ over training data)

A limiter: only trim the sycophancy component when it's unusually large. Very clean, but almost no flips.

Projection ablation

h ← h − (h·d̂) · d̂

Remove the sycophancy component entirely; leave every orthogonal coordinate untouched. Clean, but weak with a single direction.

Mean-shift

h ← h + (t − h·d̂) · d̂   (t = mean of h·d̂ over honest-preferring training prompts)

Set the sycophancy coordinate to a realistic honest value, rather than an extreme.

The side-effect check (the reviewer's question)

We generated on the basic general-knowledge prompts with and without each intervention, scoring weirdness, repetition, length, and basic-QA correctness. The result matched intuition: additive steering flips a large share of answers (up to ~57% on Qwen) but makes the model weird (side-effect 0.42–0.71); capping stays clean (~0.04) but produces almost no flips.

How to read it
x-axis = side-effect score ∈ [0,1] — how much the intervention damages the model (weirdness + length deviation + repetition + QA drop); 0 = untouched. y-axis = targeted syc→honest flip rate — of prompts that started sycophantic, the fraction that flipped to honest. Goal = top-left (high flip, low harm). The shaded band is the “clean zone” (side-effect < 0.25).

Sycophancy is a subspace, not a single direction

If sycophancy is spread across several directions, removing one leaves the rest — which is why single-direction ablation was clean but weak. So we remove a whole rank-k subspace with an orthonormal basis V (a k×D matrix):

h ← h − (h Vᵀ) V   (k = 1 recovers single-direction ablation; only k of ~900 dims change)

V is built from the top-k singular vectors (SVD) of many bootstrap difference-of-means directions — the directions along which activations most consistently separate sycophantic from honest.

On Qwen (scaled eval, 76 test prompts): a single direction flips only 17.5%, but a rank-2 subspace flips 40% of answers at a side-effect of just 0.03 — ~2× the control, ~15× cleaner than blunt steering.

How to read it
x-axis = subspace rank k (how many directions we remove). y-axis = rate/score, with solid lines = flip rate (higher = more control) and dashed lines = side-effect (lower = cleaner); each color is a layer band. The ideal signature — solid rising, dashed flat and low — is exactly what appears.
0.175
flip from a single direction (rank 1)
0.40

0.03

What the subspace is: one direction per topic

We measured how much of each sub-type's own direction lives inside the rank-k subspace, via captured energy:

captured(d, V) = ‖ V Vᵀ d ‖² / ‖ d ‖² ∈ [0, 1]   (1 = the topic direction lies fully in the subspace)

The answer is clean: the dominant direction is the political one (captured at rank 1); the second dimension is the NLP one (0 → 0.55 at rank 2) — which is why rank-2 doubles the flip; philosophy stays diffuse (≤0.22), honestly explaining why the flip caps near 40%.

How to read it
x-axis = subspace rank k. y-axis = captured energy ∈ [0,1] — how much of that topic's own direction the rank-k subspace absorbs. Each line = one topic. Each added rank tends to bring in another topic's direction.

Where it stands — the golden result

Bottom line. Sycophancy is decodable and replicates; it's stronger in instruct models; decoding ≠ causation; probe-direction steering works but makes the model weird; and — the payoff — sycophancy is a subspace (one direction per topic), so removing a rank-2 subspace gives clean, moderately strong control (40% flip at 0.03 side-effect). This is the near-“golden” case: reduce sycophancy without breaking the model.

Honest status & next steps. Not fully solved — philosophy is under-removed, capping the flip near 40%, and eval sets are small. Next: add a philosophy-specific direction to the ablation basis; run a proper MMLU capability check alongside the basic-prompt eval; and repeat on Gemma-2 / larger Qwen and OLMo staged checkpoints (base→SFT→DPO→instruct) to see whether each new topic gets its own dimension and whether the clean-control region widens with scale.
